people.name: Patricia Gloria Stephens Due
people.description:
Patricia Gloria Stephens Due, a Florida A&M student and CORE organizer, was arrested during the February 20, 1960 Woolworth sit-in in Tallahassee. After her March 17 conviction, she and seven other protesters chose jail rather than paying fines. Due entered Leon County Jail in March and was released on May 5, 1960, after serving 49 days of a 60-day sentence. Her account of the imprisonment, commonly known as "Letter from Leon County Jail," became an important document of the student civil-rights movement.

She was still Patricia Stephens at the time of the jail-in; Patricia Gloria Stephens Due is her canonical later name. Born December 9, 1939 in Quincy, Florida, she died on February 7, 2012 in Smyrna, Georgia. Florida Memory catalogs her jail letter as "Letter From A Jailed Student."
people.charges: Sit-in at the Tallahassee Woolworth lunch counter, February 20, 1960.
people.sentence: Sixty days; with seven other protesters she chose jail over paying the fine. Entered the Leon County Jail around March 18, 1960 — the entry date is approximate — and was released May 5, 1960, the best-supported date, after serving 49 days of the 60-day sentence.

people.description: Price Chatham was a Freedom Rider reportedly born on June 5, 1931 in New Gulf, Texas — the Freedom Rides Museum identifies his birth there; East Rockaway, Long Island was where he was living, not where he was born. He worked in the motion-picture industry before joining the rides. Arrested on June 2, 1961 at the Jackson, Mississippi Trailways terminal, he was sent to the Parchman state penitentiary, where he carried on a hunger strike lasting approximately twenty-four days protesting the segregation of Black and white riders within the prison. A contemporary report indicates he was released around July 11, 1961; that date is entered as probable, pending the prison discharge register. No reliable date of death has been found.
people.charges: Breach of the peace — Freedom Ride arrival at the Jackson Trailways terminal, June 2, 1961.
people.convicted: Yes — the Jackson Freedom Rides breach-of-peace prosecution
people.sentence: Jailed and sent to Parchman, where he conducted a hunger strike of approximately twenty-four days against the segregation of riders within the prison. A contemporary report indicates release around July 11, 1961 — entered as probable, not fully verified; the prison discharge register is still needed for absolute confirmation.

people.name: Robert Lee Jenkins
people.description: Robert Lee Jenkins was a twenty-seven-year-old student at St. Louis University — his age and student status are verified by the Civil Rights Digital Library — arrested on June 7, 1961 as a Freedom Rider at the Jackson Municipal Airport in Mississippi, after flying from St. Louis with two other riders to test the airport facilities. The claim that he was chairman of St. Louis CORE is reported but has not been confirmed in dependable primary sources, and the claim that he was later acquitted on a technicality is likewise unresolved. His exact release and acquittal dates remain unresolved, so no release date is entered. Born about 1934, a year derived from his reported age; no reliable date of death has been found.
people.charges: Breach of the peace — Freedom Ride test of the Jackson Municipal Airport facilities, June 7, 1961.
people.convicted: Unresolved — a later acquittal is reported but not verified
people.sentence: Arrested June 7, 1961 at the Jackson Municipal Airport. His exact release and acquittal dates remain unresolved, so no release date is entered; the reported acquittal on a technicality is not verified.

people.aka: Terry John Sullivan; John Terry Sullivan
people.description: Terry John Sullivan was a Freedom Rider from Chicago, arrested on June 6, 1961 in Jackson, Mississippi and jailed at the Parchman state penitentiary. The Mississippi surveillance record identifies him as twenty-three, with a Chicago address — a contemporary press account called him nineteen, the likely source of the age error in earlier versions of this entry. At Parchman, he and Felix Singer were subjected to wrist restraints described as "wrist breakers" and shocked with an electric cattle prod after refusing orders. He served his full four-month sentence; Catholic Worker material places his return after release in approximately October 1961, and no exact discharge day has been located. Born about 1938, a year derived from his recorded age; no reliable date of death has been found.
people.charges: Breach of the peace — the Jackson Freedom Rides prosecution, June 6, 1961.
people.convicted: Yes — served the full four-month sentence
people.sentence: Four months, served in full at Parchman, where he and Felix Singer were subjected to "wrist breakers" and an electric cattle prod for refusing orders. Contemporary Catholic Worker material places his return after release in approximately October 1961 — entered at month precision, as no exact discharge day has been located.

people.description: Thomas Walter Gaither, born November 12, 1938 in Great Falls, South Carolina, was a Claflin College graduate and CORE field secretary who organized and trained the Friendship Junior College students behind the Rock Hill "jail, no bail" protest — he was not one of the eight Friendship students himself. Ten men were arrested at the McCrory's lunch counter on January 31, 1961; one paid his fine, while Gaither and eight Friendship students refused the fines and served the hard-labor sentence at the York County Prison Farm, becoming known collectively as the Friendship Nine. Convicted February 1, he began the sentence on February 2 and was released on March 2, 1961, two days before the nominal completion of the thirty-day term. He later earned a PhD and taught biology at Slippery Rock University in Pennsylvania from 1968 until his retirement. He died on December 23, 2024 in Prospect, Pennsylvania.
people.charges: Trespass — the January 31, 1961 sit-in at the McCrory's lunch counter in Rock Hill, South Carolina.
people.sentence: Thirty days at hard labor, refused in favor of jail in the influential "jail, no bail" protest. Began the sentence at the York County Prison Farm on February 2, 1961 and was released March 2, 1961, two days before the nominal completion of the term.
